item.title: Google DeepMind releases 10‑meter global Forest Typology map with yearly change data
item.description:
Google DeepMind releases 10‑meter global Forest Typology map with yearly change data

Google DeepMind and Google Research, together with the World Resources Institute and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis, have released Forest Typology (ForTy) 2020, a global 10‑meter resolution map that categorizes every land patch into six forest and land‑use types and provides an annual time series from 2017‑2025.

🔍 Overview

  • 10‑meter resolution global map covering every 10 × 10 m pixel on Earth.
  • Six distinct forest and land‑use categories based on FAO definitions.
  • Early‑release time series tracks changes for each year from 2017 to 2025.
  • Intended as a key baseline for the European Union’s deforestation‑free regulation.

🧩 How it works

  • Trained on about 1.7 million labeled locations compiled from expert surveys, national and regional datasets, and targeted reviews of difficult cases.
  • Uses a custom architecture designed for remote‑sensing data.
  • Primary input: AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings, compact summaries of years of satellite observations for each 10‑meter pixel, enabling detection of subtle cues such as planting patterns, growth cycles, and harvest rhythms.

📊 Classification scheme

Category Definition
Primary forest Native forest with no visible signs of human disturbance.
Naturally regenerating forest Forest that grew back on its own, e.g., after logging or fire.
Planted forest Forest that people planted or seeded and manage over long cycles.
Plantation forest Fast‑growing, intensively managed tree farms, often single‑species.
Tree crops and agroforestry Farms growing non‑wood products such as oil palm, rubber, cocoa, or fruit.
Other land All remaining land types, including grassland, cropland, cities, and water.

📈 Performance

  • Validated against more than 9,000 randomly chosen sites worldwide.
  • At each site, two trained experts examined high‑resolution imagery and satellite records to determine the true land type.
  • Accuracy: 90 % correct forest‑type classification; 95 % correct forest vs. non‑forest distinction, outperforming other global forest maps.

⚙️ Output format

  • Provides a probability score for each of the six classes rather than a simple yes/no label.
  • Users can adjust thresholds to match their needs, e.g.:
    • Companies complying with the EU Deforestation‑Free Regulation may adopt a strict confidence threshold to avoid regulatory risk.
    • Researchers estimating total forest extent may use the full probability distribution for a more nuanced view.

🚀 Availability

  • The early‑release time series for each year 2017‑2025 is publicly shared.
  • Builds on the previously released Natural Forests of the World 2020 map, which identified whether each pixel was natural forest in 2020.

💡 Why it matters

  • For the first time, stakeholders can see at 10‑meter detail worldwide not only where forest loss occurs but what replaces it (timber plantation, tree‑crop farm, or other land).
  • Supports EU regulations that require products like coffee, cocoa, palm oil, and wood to be free of recent forest conversion or degradation.
  • Offers companies and researchers a high‑resolution, probabilistic tool to assess deforestation risk and monitor forest dynamics globally.

#Forestry #RemoteSensing #AIMaps #Deforestation #EURegulation

Source: Not All Forests Are Equal: Mapping the World’s Forests

item.title: OlmoEarth v1.3 releases global 10‑m satellite embeddings and explorer
item.description:
OlmoEarth v1.3 releases global 10‑m satellite embeddings and explorer

Today the team released OlmoEarth v1.3, a state‑of‑the‑art satellite embedding model that generates a 128‑dimensional vector for every 10‑meter pixel on Earth and ships with pre‑computed global embeddings and a browser‑based explorer.

🚀 Release

  • OlmoEarth v1.3 reads a full year of Sentinel‑1 radar and Sentinel‑2/Landsat multispectral time series.
  • It outputs a 128‑dimensional vector per pixel; the first 64 dimensions can be used independently.
  • Pre‑computed annual embeddings are provided for the entire planet at 10 m resolution in both 64‑ and 128‑dimensional forms.
  • The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer lets anyone pan, flip years, and compare vectors without signing in or advanced technical knowledge.

🧩 How it works

  • A vision transformer ingests the satellite data.
  • An Attention Pooler aggregates the data into one vector per land patch.
  • A linear layer reduces the pooled representation to 128 numbers.

📊 Evaluation & Performance

Variant Dimensions Leads on evals (out of 27)
OlmoEarth v1.3 (full) 128 20
OlmoEarth v1.3 (half) 64 18
  • The 128‑dimensional embeddings scored highest on 20 of 27 evaluations and ranked highest overall against AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and Tessera v2.
  • The 64‑dimensional version still led on 18 of 27 evaluations.
  • A new PLANTEUR crop‑type benchmark for tropical farming was introduced; OlmoEarth embeddings generalized best to unseen locations.

⚙️ Key details

  • Training cost: roughly $2,720 of rented H100 GPU time for the final run.
  • Compared to v1.2, training time dropped to 53% and carbon emissions to 50%; compared to v1, time dropped to 18% and emissions to 22%.
  • Model weights, pre‑training data, and code are fully open on Source Cooperative.

📈 Availability & Tools

  • The pre‑computed embeddings are shared publicly; users can train a small classifier locally for tasks such as:
    • Smallholder‑crop classification in Kenya
    • Brick‑kiln detection west of Dhaka
    • Fire‑damage assessment in Indonesia
    • Gold‑mining monitoring in the Peruvian Amazon
  • The Embeddings Explorer renders the embeddings as a false‑color map, allows year‑to‑year comparison, and lets users click a location to find similar places or drop labeled points to train a classifier on the fly.

💡 Why it matters

  • Global embeddings turn heavyweight satellite analysis into lightweight, locally‑run models.
  • In Peru’s Madre de Dios region, the embeddings highlighted illegal gold‑mining expansion from 2017‑2020 and subsequent shifts through 2025, matching on‑the‑ground reports from MAAP and the Associated Press.
  • By lowering compute and expertise barriers, the release aims to democratize high‑resolution Earth observation for research, NGOs, and industry.

#Satellites #Embeddings #OpenSource #GeospatialAI

Source: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet

item.title: HZDR Introduces SHABA: Satellite Tool for Seasonal Vegetation Analysis
item.description:
HZDR Introduces SHABA: Satellite Tool for Seasonal Vegetation Analysis

Researchers at the Helmholtz‑Zentrum Dresden‑Rossendorf (HZDR) have unveiled SHABA – Seasonal Harmonic Anomaly Break Analysis – a satellite‑based remote sensing tool designed to analyze spatial and temporal vegetational dynamics (DOI: 10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2026.07.001).

🔍 Overview

  • SHABA is a satellite‑based innovative tool for studying vegetation.
  • It was created by a research team at HZDR to better assess the spatial extent of mining facilities and their environmental impact.

🧩 How it works

  • The method factors in seasonal fluctuations and trends.
  • By incorporating these seasonal harmonics, SHABA can reliably detect and quantify changes in vegetation over time.

⚙️ Key details

  • Satellite‑based: Uses remote‑sensing data from Earth observation satellites.
  • Seasonal analysis: Explicitly models seasonal patterns to avoid misinterpreting normal cycles as anomalies.
  • Anomaly detection: Identifies breaks in expected seasonal behavior, signaling real vegetation changes.
  • Application focus: Tailored for evaluating mining‑related environmental impacts.

🚀 Availability

  • The tool is described in a peer‑reviewed article (DOI: 10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2026.07.001).
  • It represents a new capability for researchers and regulators to monitor vegetation dynamics.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables more precise assessments of how mining activities affect surrounding ecosystems.
  • Provides a systematic way to separate normal seasonal variation from actual environmental change.
  • Supports policymakers and industry with reliable data for environmental decision‑making.

#remotesensing #vegetation #satellite #AI #environment

Source: Press Releases - Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf
